idiom_name: instanceof pattern test against per-element visitor interfaces
implementation_notes: Java realises the pattern exactly as Martin's listings describe: an empty marker interface ModemVisitor as the degenerate base, one interface per element (ZoomVisitor, HayesVisitor) extending it and declaring a single visit method, and an accept whose body is if (visitor instanceof ZoomVisitor v) v.visit(this);, where the else case is simply the visitor that cannot visit this element. The acyclic win is that Zoom names only ZoomVisitor, so adding an element does not force existing visitors to be edited - the iluwatar reference implementation even combines several element interfaces into an AllModemVisitor convenience interface for visitors that handle everything. Since Java 21 the language-blessed replacement for classic Visitor is a sealed hierarchy plus a pattern-matching switch, which is closed by construction and therefore the separate sealed-hierarchy row; keep the classic Visitor when the element set is stable and compile-time coverage is worth more than openness.
pitfalls: instanceof against an interface matches any implementation, including one that implements ZoomVisitor without meaning to be a modem visitor, so keep the element-visitor interfaces narrowly named and single-method.

The marker interface must stay empty; adding a default method that logs unhandled visitors looks convenient but turns the pattern back into a classic visitor and hides which elements a visitor supports.
Adding an element changes existing visitors silently: they skip the new type instead of failing to compile, so the only defence is an explicit else branch plus tests that assert the unhandled case.
